utterances.text: Professor, if you remember, we were dealing with the decisions of the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina dated the 13th, 14, and 15th October 1991. Kindly tell us which specific moves were made at the time due to which you said were made following the proclamation of sovereignty? Which documents were issued?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: By the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I meant, Professor, by the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was objected to by the Serb deputies.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Okay. There were two documents in particular. They -- one is referred to as the letter; and the other is referred to, I think, is the declaration. Basically - and I say "basically" meaning in a summary fashion - said that the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was going to act independently in its own interests from -- from there on in, which was -- almost a declaration of independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that, following this decision by the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia issued its decision which states that soldiers from Bosnia and Herzegovina should no longer be sent to serve their military term with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Serb deputies, dissatisfied with this outvoting, did they actually walk out of the assembly session on the 13th, 14th, and 15th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, there was a walkout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about this? Ms. Bibles, I see you're nodding no. Mr. Stojanovic, if there's no dispute about it, why deal with the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'll move on, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, are you familiar with the date when the Deputies Club meeting with held - Serbian Deputies Club meeting - was held when the decision was made to establish the Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That was -- the meeting we discussed in my previous testimony. That was the 24th of October. Let me just as to the -- the answer to my previous question. What technically happened at that session of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was that Momcilo Krajisnik, who was the presiding officer as the president of the assembly, adjourned the session because he as the other Serbian deputies were against having those two documents adopted, and they then left. And the -- but the deputy president of the assembly reconvened the session, and that reconvened session passed the documents. So whether you want to call it a walkout or not is a semantic question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Professor, can I ask a question. You said when you elaborate now -- this is at page 48, line 24. You said the assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Was that the assembly or was it the assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a page of the report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 48 [sic] on the screen, line 24. Start at line 23. You say: "The Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not seeing paragraph 48 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's not a paragraph. It's the transcript of [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page, page, the transcript on the -- page 48 of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, okay. I see the page numbers now, Your Honour. I wasn't familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Page 48, line ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 24. Start from line 22.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- [Overlapping speakers] ... the assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The socialist republic, yes, that's correct. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We just made it to have it still on the screen so that you could read it. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to conclude, Professor, that the Deputies Club meeting, Serb Deputies Club meeting, which preceded the decision to establish the Serbian Assembly, was actually a response to what had been issued on the 15th of October that year, that is to say, a week earlier, by the non-Serb deputies in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, that -- that's a very complex issue, I think. I mean, on one level, yes, you could say that -- that that was the response. However, these events did not develop simply on the surface. Things happened one day and then people react the next day because of what happened the day before. The -- as I indicated earlier, the -- the various political parties had their -- had their own goals. Everyone knew everyone else's positions on the various matters of the day. And they were all able to -- to try lay various plans. I think on one occasion Radovan Karadzic said that they had their plans laid out nine steps ahead or something like that. So they knew -- the Serbian leadership, Bosnian Serb leadership knew that this was going to happen, and they thought about they were going to do and in terms of what they wanted to do anyways. And this -- the -- the actual adoption of these documents gave them a -- a very good opportunity to -- to do something that they would have done in any case, absent -- absent the agreement of the other political parties to perhaps curtail their objectives and to move in a direction more acceptable to -- to the Bosnian Serbs. Just very shortly before the adoption of -- of these documents, there had been negotiations with -- between Radovan Karadzic and Alija Izetbegovic, the head of the SDA, who was also a member of the -- the -- the Presidency. In fact, he was the president of the Presidency of the -- of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In -- Radovan Karadzic thought that Izetbegovic had come around, in fact, to accepting the idea of regionalisation of Bosnia, and he was very euphoric about that because that seemed to be an indication that negotiations were -- were heading in a favourable direction. But the -- and the final adoption of these documents showed that that was not in fact the case, and things were not going the way that the Bosnian Serbs wanted them to go but rather were back on the old track, if I can put that way. And so that they moved ahead in a fashion, again, which I think they had decided they were going to do in any case much earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you would put focused questions to the witness, then -- then we might get a bit shorter answers because the witness is almost unable to understand what exactly he is supposed to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness actually provided his answer in the very first sentence, and then it was my impression that he felt the need to expand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, Professor, can you tell us if you know when Croatia made its decision to secede from the SFRY and when did it declare its independence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any dispute about this Mr. Stojanovic? Apparently not. Let's not waste or time --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is no dispute, I will use that as a lead up to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On 8 October 1991, that is to say, a week prior to, as you put it, the controversial assembly session of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia decided to go its own way. The question is as follows. Did that decision of the neighbouring republic, which was still party to the SFRY, also have something to do with the decision made by the Bosnia-Herzegovina assembly to declare its independence?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I would think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that no one, according to the then-constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, could simply lead a people out of that republic without -- or against its will? Can they simply be excluded, so to say?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I -- I -- I don't know what the mechanism would have been according -- by which the -- the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the ones that were recognised in the constitution, as I think we've seen, could -- could have, under that constitution and in accordance with that constitution, expressed their -- their will. The -- the assembly of the republic, which was the highest body in the republic, the assembly elected the government, so the assembly was the -- the main embodiment of the sovereignty of the people or the peoples of the republic, was composed of members who were elected from various constituencies and they were not elected by nationality. They were not elected as representatives of particular -- of a particular people. They were elected as individuals. They were elected as -- as candidates of political parties, to be sure. There was an amendment to the constitution of the Socialist Republic that provided for the foundation or the creation of a -- I believe they refer to it as a council of nationalities which would have provided a -- a certain mechanism in -- in the political arena for the expression of the will of nationality -- of peoples per se, as people, as Serbs, Croats, and Muslims; however, that -- that council was in fact never created. So there -- there really wasn't a mechanism by which the -- any people -- any one people or all of them could have expressed their -- their political will as peoples to do anything of the sort that are you describing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I understand the answer. I do not fully understand the question, to be quite honest: No one, according to the then-constitution, could simply lead a people out of that republic, I do understand the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, without or against its will. Can they simply be excluded. Now, it seems to me that you have some situation on your mind. Could you be concrete and tell us to whom you referred when you said "no one," apparently have you on your mind that someone tried to, and then which people was led out of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's -- could -- could you be concrete so that I know. If you say could the Serbs do this or could the Muslims do that or could a party do that or could a parliament in incomplete composition do something? That's all language I understand. This is totally foreign to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my question was this: Could they be taken out of the SFRY? But given the professor's answer, I'd like to go back to my original question. Let me try to be direct and more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. That changes the question completely. We're dealing with a totally different question. But it still doesn't make it concrete. Do you lead a people out of the SFRY; or do you lead a constituent republic out of the SFRY? And who did it? That is all -- you need concrete starting points for your question. And when the witness started answering, you should have thought about whether -- either you misspoke or you were mistranslated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'll try to be as direct as possible. The decision made by the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated the 15th of October, 1995, does it directly contravene Article 5 of the constitution of the SFRY? You have had occasion to see it at the very beginning of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, again, without venturing a legal opinion, I would say that it was certainly viewed that way by many people at that time. Especially many Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the controversy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next question, Professor. Having in mind the provision of Article 3 of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- could, it, the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina make that decision against the will of one constituent people? The people in question being the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, that was the thrust of the answer I gave before, is there was no mechanism actually in operation by which the peoples could express their will as peoples. It was -- it was simply a vote in the assembly as members of the assembly. They voted. It was a majority. And it was passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's deal with that issue then. Do you know, Professor, whether it was by that time that Europe had established the Venice Commission which was supposed to deal with such legal matters in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that a so-called Badinter commission did have a position regarding this very issue concerning the decision made by the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina? If you're aware of their position, do share it with us; if not, just say so, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. They were issued a number of decisions. I can't remember the numbers. They are usually referred to as number 1, number 2, and that sort of thing. The decisions you're referring to I believe were in January 1992, by which time there had been application by the government of the Socialist Republic to the EU or the commission for recognition. However, as I indicated in my earlier testimony, the Bosnian Serb Assembly had been very active in bringing its point of view before the -- the European authorities so that they were aware of the fact that these steps were controversial inside Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the -- the Badinter commission basically requested that further steps be taken to confirm the will of the people in -- in Bosnia and Herzegovina to be independent. In other words, that they didn't want to simply accept the decision of -- of the -- the government who had sent them their application in December, or even the earlier decision of the assembly, which was not technically the same thing. But -- or the independently conducted referendum that the Bosnian Serbs did hold in November on this very issue in which they overwhelmingly voted to remain within Yugoslavia. A referendum which was not part of the constitutional procedure, and the Badinter commission said that -- the -- among the steps that they would like to see would be another referendum in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a general referendum on that question. And that that referendum was in fact held. So the -- just to perhaps wrap that up with this idea of peoples, that referendum that was held was -- was a general referendum and it was designed that way. It was not held by peoples. The -- most -- the SDS leadership encouraged Serbs not to vote in that referendum because they had already had their own referendum. However, the European authorities accepted the results of that referendum as a valuable expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I will ask you about that. Thank you. Let me just continue my line of questioning. Do not hold it against me for interrupting you, but we will get to the topic. Please briefly direct your attention at paragraph 171 of your report; P3003. Because have you mentioned just that, the referendum, as you called it, held by the Serbian people. There, you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, are you invited to stay a little bit further away from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, paragraph 171.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we just wait for a moment until we get the B/C/S version on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There, you say that a decision was made on 18 October 1991 at the Deputies Club meeting to hold a plebiscite of the Serb people, which would confirm the decisions made at the assembly session of the Serb people, the constituent assembly session, on the 24th of October with regard to remaining in Yugoslavia. The plebiscite was, indeed, held on 9 and 10 October, 1991. And let me ask you this, and you can see it in your footnote, specifically, and I believe we will be able to agree. It was not the referendum. Its title was plebiscite. Do you see any difference in terms of status between the two institutes in the sense of the weight to be attached to the decision made by the certain people in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a result of it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: They certainly did call it a plebiscite. I -- I think there was a technical difference between a plebiscite and a referendum. I'm not sure what it is. I could speculate. I'm sure that the lawyers in the room would have a better idea about that. But they certainly did call it a plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court, according to your information, what was the result, the outcome of the plebiscite with respect to the decision of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina to remain living in this Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the relevant paragraph says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, Professor, let me go back to what we discussed earlier. Did the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, taking into account the suggestions of the Badinter commission, take a decision on-calling a referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And it took place on the 29th of February and the 1st of March, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Your Honours, let's retrieve from e-court 65 ter document 1D01478. Let's focus on the following page in the English version. The amendment 62 where the authorities of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina by way of amendment 62 state: [As read] "The territory of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is integral and indivisible. The borders of the republic may be changed by a decision of the Assembly of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Republic only in keeping with the will of the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the basis of a previous expression of their will by way of a referendum if at least two-thirds of the total number of voters should vote in favour of changing the borders." My question to you, Professor, is: Did the constitution and this constitutional amendment foresee any way of changing the borders within Bosnia-Herzegovina against the will of two-thirds of the people living in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I'm just seeing the amendment now. It wasn't on the screen before. And that's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interject. We heard a few minutes ago that this was called a plebiscite and not a referendum, and that article, that amendment now refers to participation in a referendum. Does that make any difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that a question for me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. The -- in -- in terms of this -- of this amendment, and perhaps general terminology the Serbian plebiscite would not have qualified under this amendment. It was something, as I think I indicated, was carried out -- outside the framework of the constitution. Not to say that it wasn't a valid expression of the will of most Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stojanovic, it seems that in ordinary language, not in a technical sense, a plebiscite and a referendum are often considered to be the same. Whereas, sometimes in the various constitutional systems there may be difference. Now, you raised the issue of a different effect from plebiscite to referendum. Would you be -- would you tell us what exactly, when raising this issue, what you, in the language you're using now, what you consider to be the difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I personally, not dealing with semantics, would say that the goal and the meaning of both decisions was the same, and that is the peoples' expression of their will on certain political and legal issues and thereby gathering support for a certain political decision. In this particular case, Defence holds that the referendum entitled "A Plebiscite," semantically plebiscite has a wider scope than referendum because plebiscite means the expression of all and the referendum is something which provides a certain answer to a question. Was entitled "A Plebiscite" because of the current political needs that dictated and informed the decisions of both assemblies. Both the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think this what I wanted to elicit from the professor as a reply, that there was reason behind the decision of the 9th and 10th of October that bore the title "plebiscite."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm going to interrupt you. I'm still puzzled by the beginning of what you said. Defence holds that the referendum entitled "A Plebiscite," semantically has a wider scope because a plebiscite refers to all and a referendum is something which provides a certain answer to a question which are two totally incomparable matters. It is like saying a market-place is where many people gather and where vegetables are sold is a market-place. I mean, the one is about the question, and the other one is about who are consulted on that question. So, therefore, you're at least confusing me. It may be that I'm not listening carefully enough. But could you please, again without a long explanation, say what is the difference between a plebiscite and a referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me reiterate: It is my upon in this specific case that decision does not exist, in essence, that both are expressions of a will on a specific issue put forward. But with your leave, by the same token, I do believe that there was a current political reason because behind the decision not to call the expression of will on the 9th and 10th of October a referendum but, rather, a plebiscite. And this is far as I'm willing to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what are you now saying is, it is, as a matter of fact, the same, but there were political reasons to make a distinction? Okay. If it ... I hope that it ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you asked the witness what were the consequences of calling it the one or the other. So you're asking the witness whether two things that are the same get a -- have a different consequences or different impact, because current political reasons existed to consider it not to be the same. That is a pretty complex question. Again, I don't understand, to start with, the question; and that is part of what happens at this moment, that the witness explains patiently a lot of things he thinks are more or less related to your questions, questions which are often unclear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me provide a quick answer by asking this question. Professor, who was the actor within the constitution and legal system of Bosnia-Herzegovina who is entitled to take a decision on calling a referendum?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I would think that be the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the decision on a plebiscite on the 9th and 10th of October, who did take that decision?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That was taken by the Assembly of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, pursuant to the constitution, could not have taken a decision on referendum, but the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina could?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just help me follow your questions, Mr. Stojanovic. You've just told us that there is, semantically speaking, there is no difference between a plebiscite and a referendum. Judge Orie has tried to go to length to follow your logic on this. We still didn't understand what you said except to say that they don't -- they mean the same thing except when political conditions existed made them mean differently, and you didn't tell us what are those conditions that made them to mean differently and what that different meaning is. Now, when you asked this question, I would like for me to be able to understand to, I would like you to explain what do you mean when you used the word "plebiscite" and what do you mean when you used the word "referendum"? Can you please do that, because I don't understand and I'm not going to understand the answer that comes from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me reiterate. In the opinion of the Defence, both mean the expression of a will of a group or the entire population of a state. What is the difference? Pursuant to the then-constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a decision on a referendum may be taken only exclusively by the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If you call something a referendum and you wish that decision to be legal, then it must be taken by the legal institution or organ. If you call something a plebiscite because you want one group within that state to make their will known, then you do not require a decision by the competent organise of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And therein lies the difference for calling the same thing two different titles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that difference you've told us. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, in essence, the answer is, a vast majority -- I asked the professor what percentage of the Serb people expressed their will at the plebiscite to remain living in Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that correct, Professor, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: If the question is did the vast majority express their will to remain within Yugoslavia, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask another question. What percentage of the total population of Bosnia-Herzegovina did the Serbian population constitute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were about 31 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you this, Professor. Did you collect official information in light of amendment 62? What was the official result of the referendum that took place on the 29th of February and March 1st, 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I -- I can't remember the -- the precise figures. I think it's mentioned in the report. It was published in the Official Gazette. It's -- it -- showing was a majority, but I can't remember the percentage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't -- is there any dispute about the percentages and is the outcome of this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the issue is was it more than two-thirds or not, I'm sorry, I just can't remember whether it was more than two-thirds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No dispute, Ms. Bibles?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No dispute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, usually these kind of things, either there is a real dispute about the outcome. Then focus on that. Or there is no dispute and then follow what was published at the time as the outcome. But don't spend time on it with the witness, unless there's any specific issue you want to introduce through that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm -- I'm willing to stipulate if the Prosecution agrees that the result of the referendum was that less than two thirds of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina expressed their will for Bosnia-Herzegovina to be sovereign and secede from SFRY. If they would stipulate that, I would stipulate as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can ask them to stipulate. You can stipulate yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, I would accept that it was less than two-thirds of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who expressed their wish to secede from Yugoslavia on that referendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, agreed, not agreed?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Agreed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No further questions as to this matter. No need to express percentages. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So if less than two-thirds of the population expressed or voted for independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and cessation from Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, would the decision on independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina contravene the amendment 62 that you see before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, again, these -- these are legal issues which I think are pretty complicated. I note that the -- the amendment under discussion refers to changing the boundaries. I don't know whether that -- to me changing the boundaries means, like, a shifting the line between -- the boundary line between, you know, Bosnia and Croatia or something like that by a few kilometres. What we are talking about here is basically severing the connection of independence. I don't know whether that comes within the meaning of this amendment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say, it's reading the amendment 62, it is unclear to you whether that would be -- would contravene that amendment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. For the reasons you have explained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's look at 65 ter 07482; English page 18, B/C/S page 7. Article 5 of the article of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which we had an opportunity to see earlier in the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In Article 5 of the constitution of SFRY, it is stated, in paragraph 3: [As read] "Border of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia cannot be changed without the consent of all republics and autonomous provinces." Would the decision on independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina without the consent of other republics and autonomous provinces, which make up the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, would contravene article 5 of the federal constitution. You may answer with a "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, I am afraid I would have to give the same answer I gave to the previous question. It's really not clear to me what the -- changing the border means. Is it the external border, shifting the border between the SFRY and Hungary or something? Or does the independence of one of the republics come within the meaning of that? I don't know. And I would have to remark that in -- certainly at the beginning of 1992, two of the republics had already been recognised as independent states, so the idea that the -- all the republics of the -- the SFRY were going to get together and decide something was -- was something that wasn't going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now let's look together at document -- 65 ter document bearing number 16158. Please, let's focus on Article 1 of the decision on the establishment of the Republika Srpska of Bosnia-Herzegovina stated as the decision of the Third Assembly of the Serbian people held on the 21st of -- 11th of December, 1991. It is being -- it is stated that if the Serb -- if Croatia and Slovenia were to change their attitude and position towards Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that the Assembly -- well, English version is supposed to be seen on the next page, but I'm sure that you will be able to follow. Do you agree that the decision of the Third Session of the Assembly of the Serbian people is conditional and that establishment of the republic of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina will follow through only if the Croatian and Muslim community were to change their opinion towards Yugoslavia? Was that done in practice? Was this how it worked in practice?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I've -- different things have appeared on the screen. I'm not sure what we're focusing on at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm looking at something about -- about the municipal assemblies here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- Mr. Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In English. I see in B/C/S it's a decision that [Overlapping speakers] ... proceed to the formation of the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we first want Mr. Stojanovic to clearly identify what he draws the attention of the witness to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do believe we have a problem. I stopped receiving interpretation, and -- now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, then, I repeat what I said a second ago. Please assist the witness in telling him exactly what you are drawing his attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, please take a look at the decision from the 4th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the establishment of the republic of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English version does not correspond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Stojanovic, that's exactly the problem. I see in B/C/S, I see decisions which are numbered, 19, 20, 21. First of all, which one do you have on your mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 21, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 21. And at this moment, it seems that we have -- let me have a look what we have on our screen. Could we go one page -- let me -- one second. It looks as if we are looking at the bottom of 20 rather than 21. Could we move to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Preceding page, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I asked to go to the next page in English and I would wish to have a look at that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- that seems to be the last page in English. Mr. Stojanovic, do you agree that what we see at this moment on our screen ends at the left bottom, which seems to correspond with the end of number 20, that it reads: "Number 02-53-91," under that, "11 December 1991," and then "Sarajevo," whereas, at the right, it seems that it is originating from Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, and it seems that this all corresponds. If you want to take us to number 21, you have to provide an English translation for 21, which apparently is not uploaded into e-court. That's where we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do believe that you're right. Maybe it would a good time to go for a break, and then in the meantime I'll try to provide an English translation with apologies, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And -- well, English translation is more important even than apologies. We take a break, Mr. Treanor, and we would like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom again. Would it be a good idea if the parties would try to reach an agreement on what portions of what constitutions they want to rely upon and then to have them in evidence to the extent we need them? Okay. Mr. Stojanovic, were you able to find a translation for what appears now on our screen to be number 21 in this -- in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thanks to our dear Janet. She was successful in identifying the translation. I would kindly ask Janet to help us with e-court as well, to see the English translation on the screens. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I will repeat the question I had for you when we still did not have the English translation. It is one of the decisions of the 4th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 21st of December, 1991. It is in item 1: "Preparations are to be made to set up the Republic of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina as a federal unit within the federal state of Yugoslavia, if the Croatian and Muslim ethnic communities decide to change their attitude towards Yugoslavia." While conducting your analysis and preparation for your testimony -- in preparation for your testimony, did you also arrive at some kind of knowledge about the decision on the establishment -- sorry, the establishment of Republika Srpska was made under certain preconditions and it had been directly linked to the position taken by the Croat and Muslim communities?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, yes. As I indicated there were negotiations going on in late 1991/early 1992. The SDA and the HDZ had taken certain steps in the assembly and in -- after this decision, the -- their government -- the government that they nominated requested recognition from the EU, and the -- this is -- this document is predicated on the hope which I quite like -- may likely, the Bosnian Serbs leadership, would not likely would have seen as vain, perhaps, that the HDZ and the SDA would not do that, but they did in, as I said, on about the 21st of December, and therefore, on the 9th of January, they -- the Bosnian Serb Assembly adopted its declaration on the establishment of the republic, because the -- the Croats and the Muslims had -- had -- persisted in their quest for independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, Professor, that in all of the constituent acts starting with the declaration and ending with the constitution of Republika Srpska, there is a clear indication of the position of the Serb people which was its wish to remain within the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that in the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there's a constitutional provision which states that Republika Srpska was to remain part of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And that remained unchanged even after the declaration of independence of the Bosnian Serb republic, at the beginning of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could I just try to -- I do understand that - let me just have a look - that you wanted to take us to that number 21, if I'm understanding you well what -- of what we earlier had on our screen. Now we have now e-court which seems to be a decision, and that refers to that number 21. But could you look in the original B/C/S, because I think there are -- only half of that decision appears. Because we're now looking at the English. But going back to what you showed us earlier --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the B/C/S version, this decision has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me have a look now what we have on our screen now. We have this number 21, but only the first and the second paragraph or sub-articles there. Now, where is the remainder of the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page in the B/C/S containing a provision of Article 3. I believe it's before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I have a look at that next page. Because in e-court, as far as I can see it, that page does not follow the one we have on our screen now. So we started with a part of number 21 without an English translation. We now have a full English translation of that number 21 but no full original. I see that you're helplessly looking around but ... Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour. I may be able to cast some light on the difficulties we have. The Prosecution Exhibit, which originally was called up in this case, I believe that is 65 ter 16158, is actually the 20th Session we see in the B/C/S original. And so the English translation matches the 20th. So, over the break, Ms. Stewart was able to find the full translation of the 21st Session, which is what she brought up on the screen so I'm -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I can interrupt you. I fully understand that the Prosecution supported Mr. Stojanovic to the best of its abilities. But Mr. Stojanovic should have checked before he came to court whether he had a full original B/C/S and a full translation. Because the one page, which only gives 19 and 20 in full, Mr. Stojanovic, may have been uploaded by the Prosecution for totally different purposes, and they may not have been interested in number 21. Whereas, if you are, you should take care that it's there in its entirety with a translation. Please proceed, but the Chamber is not much inclined to work on the basis of half originals with full translations. If they correspond, because they can't check that. But 21 seems to be very much the same as what apparently Ms. Stewart has provided us with. Perhaps you move on and sort this out and go to your next subject and see, at the end, whether you are in a position to, again, deal with this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I'll move on. Although, I have to admit, that I had the other page in paper copy. But now I see that in e-court the next page in B/C/S is, indeed, missing. It was my omission. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, bearing in mind what we have discussed about the decision, can we next, together, look at P3007, which was a decision on the promulgation of the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You have had occasion to see this during examination-in-chief as well. In the English, could we go to the next page, please. Bearing in mind your last answer that, in all of the constituent documents, Republika Srpska insisted on remaining part of the SFRY. In that regard, do focus your attention on Article 4, which reads that: "The republic may enter into associations with state forms of other peoples constitutive of Bosnia-Herzegovina." This is from the RS constitution. Can you see that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this keeping with the decision we saw a moment ago on the establishment of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if the Muslim and Croat peoples take a different direction?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, this -- this article, I guess, would become operative once the -- the Croatian and Muslim peoples decided to ... leave Yugoslavia, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let us look together at a provision of paragraph 245, as well as paragraph 246 of your report, which is P3003. You've already discussed it. Paragraphs 245, 246, and 247. Under the provisions of the Law on the Armed Forces, as you define it in those paragraphs, the Supreme Commander of the armed forces was the president of the republic. He commands the armed forces in keeping with the law and the constitution. By virtue of changes to the Presidency, whereby the number of members increased from three to five, and then we also had the president of the republic with two vice-presidents, did anything change? In other words, the regulations dealing with the issues of the armed forces and commanding the armed forces, did they undertake any changes with respect to the Supreme Commander and who the Supreme Commander was to be?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: The -- no, I don't believe there were any changes. The Supreme Commander remained the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During your work, did you familiarise yourself with the notion of the Supreme Command and who comprised it? The Supreme Command of the armed forces in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who comprised the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, the Supreme Command, as -- as established at the end of 1992 - and I'm doing this from my memory; I believe it's in the report - included the -- the members of the Presidency, as it existed at that time and the ministers of internal affairs, foreign affairs, and defence perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that, in late 1992, as part of the constitutional and legal system of Republika Srpska, the Presidency no longer existed as a collective body. It was, rather, the president with two vice-presidents.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. As of 17 December 1992, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we also agree that the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of RS was not a member of the command, the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask that we look together at paragraph 263 of the same document; P3003. In paragraph 263, Professor, you say the following: "Despite the fact that a state of war was never officially declared, apparently for political reasons, there are multiple additional indications that an expanded Presidency was in fact in operation after 1 June 1992." Do tell the Court, please, what you meant by saying that "a state of war was never officially declared apparently for political reasons."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, a state of war never was declared, and there's -- in the document that's referenced, in that footnote, the contents of which I specifically cannot remember at this time, there was apparently indication -- the why that did not happen. This was all that that document was probably issued within the context of the discussion about the -- the -- the documents that -- the normative documents that underlay the -- the exist of the expanded Presidency. This -- there's a lot of discussion in the report about the fact that it mention the state of war, imminent threat of war, or didn't mention imminent threat of war, and so there was a feeling that there had been some discrepancy between the documentation, the laws, as -- as they had been adopted in early June 1992 and the actual operation of the Presidency and that something should be done about that, and one of the suggestions was to go back and amend the laws, the constitutional law, to insert the words "imminent threat of war" which would cover the current situation because there was no state of war for -- that -- I think that document says for political reasons. But, instead, they decided to reform the institution of the Presidency entirely by creating a -- having one president and two vice-presidents on the 17th of December. What the specific political reasons were, I don't -- I don't -- I don't know. I -- I could only speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to make sure that I understand you. In your report, you say that it will -- happened apparently for political reasons and that, for those reasons, the authorities in Republika Srpska never officially declared a state of war. In your view, what were the political reasons due to which a state of war was never declared?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you've listened well, you would have heard the witness say: "What the specific political reasons were... I don't know ... I could only speculate." Therefore, the witness apparently observes that a war is going on, on the ground, that a state of war was not declared, and that he thinks that there were political reasons on which he can only speculate, which we usually do not encourage witnesses to do. Therefore, your question is a repetitive one. Unless you want to hear the speculations of the witness, the Chamber is, as you know, usually not interested in speculations. Unless the witness knows certain facts which he links to what he thinks possibly may have been reasons. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you referred to footnote 729, where you say that, in terms of your conclusion, one should look at unedited working material for the reports about the work of the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the period April to June 1992, as well as Presidency minutes from the 30th November 1992 session. Did you find a specific answer in those documents to the question why no state of war was declared?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what the witness said twice, and you're asking him again. Apparently the footnote is relevant. You can ask the witness what he found in that footnote that supported his conclusion that there likely were political reasons. But he said: I don't know what those reasons are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When was the decision on proclaiming an immediate threat of war issued?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: It was issued on the 15th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the decision was made one month later, in May 1992. Was this a mistake, or do you have some specific knowledge regarding when it was published as opposed to when it was made? When did it enter into force?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, my recollection is that it was -- the decision was taken on the 15th of April and entered into force on that date. It was published in the Official Gazette, so ... it would be easy to consult that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now let's clarify one issue that you referred to in your report, and that is the issue of the ad hoc organs established in Republika Srpska. First and foremost, the issue of the National Security Council. What kind of an organ was that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I -- I take it you're referring to the National Security Council that was formed in 1992. It was formed as a -- as an advisory body basically. There -- there's a -- an issue surrounding the decision creating it in that decision was never published in the Official Gazette, but the -- the -- the form that's cited in the report comes from the stenographic record of the assembly session at which it was adopted. Because there was lot of discussion about the National Security Council and what it should be, and it appears from that stenographic record that the decision was adopted in the form in which it appears in that record, and it is referred to as an advisory body in -- in that decision. If I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your work, did you notice that the National Security Council, at any point, was established or constituted, and that it issued any proposals or initiatives in keeping with its purview?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, the -- the -- the council did begin to meet. We have some minutes of those meetings which are discussed in the report. It -- it would -- or it -- after its discussions, decisions would be issued in the name of the -- the two acting presidents of the republic, who were members of the council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that that council at any point represented place, a forum, where important political military decision would be either taken or proposed, such that would be of import for the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was nobody from the military personnel as part of that National Security Council; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say that's correct. I -- I believe the minister of defence was a member, who was a military person, and he was also designated by the -- by the council to be at least the acting commander of the Territorial Defence at the end of April. The Territorial Defence being the only armed force, the only military force that the republic had at that time. It had the police, of course, but this is before the army was created on the 12th of May, so it only had the Territorial Defence. And, again, the minister of defence, who became the -- the commander of the Territorial Defence, was a member of the council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, it's time to adjourn for the day. Mr. Treanor, we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at quart -- half past 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before I ask you to be escorted out of the courtroom, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way, with whomever, about your testimony, whether that is testimony given today or testimony still to be given tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'd like to see you back tomorrow. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I think you used approximately two hours. Are you on track, as far as time is concerned? Which would mean that you would finish in the first session tomorrow. One hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, by all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 3rd of December, 9.30, in the Courtroom III -- I misspoke. Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 3rd day of December, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.16 p.m.,
